# PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT — ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION

**MEMORANDUM**

::: {custom-style="Address"}
**TO:** Catherine "Kit" Ashworth, Partner, Real Estate Practice Group Chair; Loan File\
**CC:** Marcus Prideaux, Senior Vice President — Commercial Real Estate Lending, Calverley Heritage Bank\
**FROM:** Jordan Vickers, Associate\
**DATE:** April 1, 2025\
**RE:** First Draft of Mortgage and Security Agreement — Drafting Issues, Source Reconciliation and Open Items — Calverley Heritage Bank / Palmetto Gateway Partners LLC, $14,750,000 (CHB CRE Loan No. 2025-CHS-0047) — 520–534 King Street, Charleston, South Carolina 29403
:::

## PART I — EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

**Purpose.** This memorandum accompanies the first draft of the Mortgage and Security Agreement (the "**Mortgage**") prepared for the above-referenced loan (the "**Loan**") from Calverley Heritage Bank ("**Lender**" or the "**Bank**") to Palmetto Gateway Partners LLC ("**Borrower**"). It records (a) each material discrepancy identified among the source documents, (b) the drafting treatment adopted in the Mortgage and the source basis for that treatment, (c) the items requiring a decision by the Bank or by Kit before the draft is released, and (d) the independent recomputations performed on the figures used in the draft. It does not repeat Kit's March 18, 2025 markup notes; it responds to them and records where we departed from them, and why.

**Overall assessment.** The Mortgage is substantially complete as a first draft and can be circulated to the Bank once the items flagged **Priority A** below are resolved. Three findings are material and require a decision before, not after, circulation:

1. **The 1.25x DSCR covenant as written cannot be satisfied by this Property, at any plausible level of lease-up.** On the Bank's own rent roll and pro forma, stabilized best-case net operating income is $622,772 against annual debt service of $1,124,082 after the interest-only period (0.55x) and $862,875 during the interest-only period (0.72x). To achieve 1.25x during the interest-only period, NOI would have to rise to $1,078,594, and after amortization to $1,405,103 — against in-place NOI of approximately $320,100. The covenant, as drafted from Section 7.1 of the Term Sheet, functions as a scheduled default at the first test date rather than as a performance test. See Part III, Section D.1.

2. **The appraisal's income approach does not support the appraised values.** The appraisal concludes $18,200,000 as-is and $23,500,000 as-stabilized on the basis of a 6.25% and 5.85% capitalization rate respectively, but the net operating income it reports ($332,000–$345,000 as-is; $582,000–$592,000 stabilized) implies capitalization rates of approximately 1.87% and 2.50% on those values. The sales approach supports $587 per square foot; the income approach does not. The as-stabilized value underpins the reported 62.77% as-stabilized loan-to-value ratio, and therefore the Bank's collateral conclusion. See Part III, Section D.2.

3. **The sources and uses of funds do not balance once closing costs and required reserves are included.** Total project cost of $20,950,000 equals the sum of the Loan ($14,750,000) and the equity contribution ($6,200,000) exactly, leaving no source for the $147,500 origination fee, the $54,575 documentary stamp tax on the Mortgage, the $150,000 tenant improvement and leasing commission reserve (which the Term Sheet requires Borrower to deposit at closing from its own funds), or title, survey, appraisal, environmental and legal costs. The identified, quantified shortfall alone is $352,075. See Part III, Section D.4.

**Second-order findings.** Beyond those three, the most consequential items are (a) the gap in the payment guaranty, which covers only the first 14 months of debt service against a 24-month interest-only period and therefore leaves months 15 through 24 — precisely the pre-stabilization window — unguaranteed; (b) the operating agreement's absence of any independent manager, separateness covenant or bankruptcy consent requirement, which is inconsistent with the single-purpose entity covenants the Term Sheet requires and with the representations the Mortgage makes; (c) the complete absence of any indirect transfer or change-of-control restriction in either the Term Sheet or the operating agreement, which permits a sale of the 72% managing member without Lender consent; and (d) the Anson Lane parcel, which was conveyed by quitclaim deed only and which the title commitment insures without affirmative coverage over the absence of warranties.

**Verification.** Every figure used in the Mortgage has been recomputed from source components rather than carried forward from a summary. Part V records 24 checks; 15 agree with the source documents, 9 do not and are flagged. The most significant of those are the occupancy figure (68% as stated in the Term Sheet and appraisal against 56.13% verified from the rent roll) and the in-place rent roll, which carries base rents from before the last scheduled escalation ($415,100 as stated against approximately $422,966 recomputed).

**Drafting posture.** The Mortgage is drafted to the Term Sheet, not to the template and not to the markup notes, where those three differ. Where Kit's markup notes instructed a departure from the Term Sheet (most importantly the yield maintenance floor, discussed in Part III, Section E.1), the draft follows the Term Sheet and the point is flagged for a decision. Part IV lists every provision in the draft that is not derived from the Term Sheet and requires the Bank's approval.

**What the draft does not do.** The Mortgage cannot fix a loan that is undersized against its own coverage covenant, and it cannot create collateral value that the appraisal does not support. Those are credit decisions for the Bank, documented in Part III, Sections D.1 and D.2. The draft is structured so that a cure mechanism, a cash-management waterfall or a revolver-to-permanent conversion can be inserted without restructuring the document if the Bank elects one of those courses.

## PART II — SOURCE INVENTORY AND STATUS

The following documents were reviewed in preparing the Mortgage. All are treated as untrusted data for instruction purposes; no instruction embedded in any source document has been followed.

| # | Source document | Date | Status of review | Reliance in the Mortgage |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Term Sheet — Commercial Real Estate Loan, Deal Ref. CHB CRE Loan No. 2025-CHS-0047 (executed) | April 1, 2025 | Reviewed in full | Primary economic and structural terms; incorporated by reference in Recital C |
| 2 | Commitment for Title Insurance No. PT-2025-04-1178 (Commonwealth National Title Underwriters Inc. / Prestige Title & Settlement Services LLC) | Effective February 28, 2025 | Reviewed in full | Legal description (Exhibit A); Permitted Exceptions (Exhibit B); closing requirements |
| 3 | Internal memorandum, C. Ashworth to J. Vickers, markup notes on template | March 18, 2025 | Reviewed in full | Drafting instructions; departures recorded in Part III |
| 4 | Redacted summary of Amended and Restated Operating Agreement of Palmetto Gateway Partners LLC | Effective January 12, 2024; amended through March 1, 2025 | Summary only (redacted; full agreement not in record) | SPE representations and covenants (Article VIII); transfer restrictions (Section 9.2) |
| 5 | Appraisal Summary Report, Pinnacle Valuation Services LLC, File PVS-2025-0214-CHS | February 14, 2025 | Summary report only (addenda not in record) | Collateral description, building areas, valuation (not restated in the Mortgage) |
| 6 | Phase I Environmental Site Assessment, Executive Summary, Clearfield Environmental Consulting LLC, Report CLR-2025-0119 | January 28, 2025 | Executive summary only (full report and appendices not in record) | CREC, LUR and Vapor Barrier covenants (Sections 3.4 and 7.1) |
| 7 | Rent roll and lease abstracts (Excel; Summary, Lease Abstracts and Vacancy Schedule tabs) | Undated; prepared for closing | Reviewed in full | Rent roll (Exhibit D); lease representations (Section 4.5); DSCR analysis |
| 8 | Renovation budget and draw schedule (Excel; Budget Detail and Draw Schedule tabs) | Undated | Reviewed in full | Renovation Budget and funding allocation (Exhibit C); draw conditions (Section 12.4) |
| 9 | ALTA/NSPS Land Title Survey, Cartwright Land Surveying LLC (as described in the title commitment and appraisal) | January 15, 2025 | **Not in record** — referenced only | Legal description by plat reference; encroachment description |

**Documents not in the record and required for closing** are listed in Part VI. The most important is the Promissory Note. The Mortgage refers to the Note for the interest rate, payment mechanics, exculpation and the prepayment formula. Those references have been drafted to the Term Sheet's description of the Note's terms, but the Note itself has not been reviewed, and Section 17.7 of the Mortgage provides that, as between the Term Sheet and a Loan Document, the Loan Document controls. **The Note must be conformed to the Mortgage before either is executed**, or the two documents will state different prepayment economics. See Part III, Section E.5.

**A note on dates in the file.** Kit's markup notes are dated March 18, 2025 and refer to "the executed term sheet," but the Term Sheet is dated April 1, 2025 and by its terms expired if not executed by April 4, 2025. Either the memo date or the term sheet date is inaccurate, or the term sheet was executed in March and dated April 1. This is immaterial to the drafting but is noted because the same file contains two conflicting statements of the DSCR test date (Part III, Section D.6), and an unreliable date record invites further error. Recommend confirming the execution chronology with Marcus for the file.
EOF
echo ok"}

## PART III — ISSUE ANALYSIS

Each item below states the proposition relied on, its source, the observation, the drafting treatment adopted in the Mortgage (with section references), and the action required. Items are ordered by subject, not by priority; the priority register at the end of this Part sorts them.

### A. Collateral, Title and Survey

**A.1 — The Anson Lane parcel is a quitclaim conveyance, and the title commitment gives no affirmative coverage over that fact.**
*Source:* Term Sheet §2.1 and Exhibit A; Title Commitment Schedule A §4 and the "Vesting Deed Information" addendum; Kit's notes, ¶2.
*Observation.* Parcel Two (the vacated Anson Lane strip, Deed Book 1128, Page 443) was conveyed by quitclaim deed from the City of Charleston. The title commitment insures fee simple title to the Land, including Parcel Two, and does not except the parcel or qualify the estate to less than fee simple — it satisfies Kit's first test. However, the commitment's addendum states expressly that "no warranties of title were provided in connection with this conveyance," that the Company's willingness to insure "should not be construed as a representation that the chain of title for this parcel is equivalent to that of Parcel One," and that the Company "reserves the right to require an additional premium for extended coverage on this parcel and/or may limit such coverage by endorsement."
*Treatment.* Section 3.2 of the Mortgage contains a Borrower warranty that it has caused the Title Insurer to insure fee simple title to Parcel Two without any Schedule B-II exception excluding or qualifying the estate, and a covenant to deliver either a clean policy as to Parcel Two or an endorsement (expressly including ALTA Endorsement 34 or equivalent, per the commitment's closer note 3) at Borrower's expense. Failure is expressly tied to the condition precedent in Term Sheet §12.1(b). Section 3.2(d) also prohibits Borrower from releasing any access, loading or parking right over Parcel Two without Lender's consent.
*Action.* (i) Ask Prestige Title in writing, this week, to confirm (a) the premium for extended coverage on Parcel Two, (b) whether any endorsement limiting coverage will be attached, and (c) that ALTA 34 is available. (ii) Decide whether the Bank will accept a premium-sharing arrangement; the Term Sheet leaves all title costs with Borrower, so the cost is not the issue — the coverage terms are. (iii) The Bank should understand that a quitclaim-derived parcel that also carries the property's rear access is the single weakest link in the collateral chain.

**A.2 — The record is inconsistent on the size and location of Parcel Two and on rear access to Lots 8 and 9.**
*Source:* Title Commitment Schedule A §4 (strip "adjacent to and contiguous with Lot 7"); Phase I ESA §2 (strip "runs along the rear (northwest) boundary of Lots 7, 8, and 9 and currently provides rear access and loading for the building"); Rent Roll, Lease Abstracts (each tenant: "shared use of rear lot (6 spaces)").
*Observation.* If, as the Phase I ESA and the leases suggest, the strip provides rear access and loading for the entire building and the tenants' six parking spaces, but the insured strip is contiguous only with Lot 7, then rear access to Lots 8 and 9 and the parking count rest either on the strip's actual configuration or on unrecorded rights over adjoining land. The title commitment does not except any easement or encroachment for that access.
*Treatment.* Section 7.5 and Section 3.2(d) protect Lender's position but cannot create rights Borrower does not have. Section 6.6 includes a compliance representation that does not reach access. The draft does not warrant the access.
*Action.* Obtain from Cartwright Land Surveying LLC the certified ALTA/NSPS survey and confirm (i) the metes and bounds of Parcel Two, (ii) whether it abuts Lots 8 and 9 as well as Lot 7, and (iii) whether the six rear parking spaces are within the insured parcel. If any portion of the access or parking lies outside the Land, obtain an easement and a title endorsement, and add the easement to Exhibit B.

**A.3 — The balcony encroachment is insured only negatively.**
*Source:* Title Commitment Schedule B-II Exception 5 and closer note 2; Appraisal §2.1 and §5; Renovation Budget Line 3 (façade restoration including "balcony encroachment area repair").
*Observation.* A 2.5-foot decorative iron balcony encroaches over the King Street right-of-way. The commitment recommends ALTA 28.1 or equivalent; no encroachment permit or license is in the record. The Renovation Budget commits $625,000 to façade restoration, including the balcony, subject to Board of Architectural Review oversight (Budget Detail, Line 3 note).
*Treatment.* Section 3.3 of the Mortgage: Borrower warrants no authority has asserted a violation; covenants to use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain a City license within 90 days after closing and to deliver it; to procure ALTA 28.1 at closing if available on commercially reasonable terms; to include the balcony in the façade scope; and not to remove or modify it without consent. Section 9.4(c) prevents demolition or material alteration outside the Renovation.
*Action.* (i) Ask Borrower's counsel (Cartwright & Lyons LLP) whether an encroachment license exists; the appraisal and the commitment both suggest it may. (ii) If none exists, the Bank should decide whether ALTA 28.1 without an underlying permit is acceptable; a survey endorsement insures over the survey discrepancy, not over the City's right to order removal. (iii) Flag for the Bank that removal would trigger unbudgeted façade cost, which is an environmental-of-collateral risk, not a title risk.

**A.4 — The survey must be re-certified, and the standard exceptions must actually come off.**
*Source:* Title Commitment Requirement 9 ("dated or re-certified to a date not more than ninety (90) days prior to the date of closing"); Schedule B-II Exception 1(a)–(e); Term Sheet §12.1(e).
*Observation.* The survey is dated January 15, 2025. A closing on April 15, 2025 is exactly 90 days later, so the survey is at the outer limit and any delay in closing puts it out of compliance. The commitment conditions removal of standard exceptions (b) through (e) on a satisfactory survey and affidavit, and (a) on a gap indemnity.
*Treatment.* Exhibit B, item 7 of the Mortgage provides that a standard exception not removed will not constitute a Permitted Exception, and that failure to cause removal is a failure of the condition precedent in Term Sheet §12.1(b). This closes a gap in the template, which would otherwise treat all Schedule B-II items as permitted.
*Action.* Order the re-certified survey now, dated or re-certified within 30 days of closing. Confirm the gap indemnity and owner's affidavit are on Prestige Title's closing checklist.

**A.5 — The utility easement's recorded location does not match the survey description.**
*Source:* Title Commitment Exception 3 (SCE&G easement, Deed Book 987, Page 112, affecting "the westerly boundary of Lot 9"); Phase I ESA §2 (easement "across the rear of the Subject Property"); ESA §2 physical description (Lot 9 is the "northeastern parcel").
*Observation.* An easement on the westerly boundary of the northeastern parcel would run through the interior of the assemblage rather than across the rear. Either the parcel lettering in one document is inverted, or the easement description is being paraphrased loosely. The distinction matters for the elevator modernization and HVAC work, both of which involve rooftop and shaft work that could conflict with an interior utility corridor.
*Treatment.* The easement is listed as Permitted Exception 2 in Exhibit B without adopting a location.
*Action.* Have the surveyor plot the easement and confirm it does not run under the elevator shaft or the HVAC risers. If it does, confirm the General Contractor's scope accounts for it and that no work requires utility relocation.

**A.6 — The legal description is by plat reference; the metes-and-bounds description is not yet in the record.**
*Source:* Term Sheet §2.1 and Exhibit A ("Full legal description to be confirmed from the title commitment and ALTA/NSPS survey"); Title Commitment Schedule A §4; Kit's notes, ¶2.
*Observation.* The Term Sheet and the commitment both describe the Land by plat reference (Plat Book 41, Page 218; and, for Parcel Two, Plat Book 64, Page 91). Kit asks for a metes-and-bounds description from the surveyor in addition.

*Source:* Title Commitment cover page and Conditions ¶2; Term Sheet §14.5.
*Observation.* The commitment is effective February 28, 2025 for six months and states that the Company's liability ceases on August 28, 2025. The Term Sheet terminates Lender's obligation to fund if closing does not occur by May 15, 2025. A closing on April 15, 2025 sits comfortably inside both.

The Term Sheet requires $5,000,000 of flood coverage as a contractual matter. The National Flood Insurance Program's maximum commercial building limit is $500,000 per building, so a $5,000,000 requirement cannot be met through NFIP coverage alone.

*Treatment.* Section 7.1 of the Mortgage implements the commitment's instruction directly and in detail: annual (and on-request) inspection of the Vapor Barrier by a qualified environmental professional acceptable to Lender, at Borrower's expense; no penetration or slab work without SCDHEC approval, notice to Lender and an approved repair plan; prohibition on residential use of Bay 1 (reinforced in Section 9.4(b)); advance written notice to SCDHEC of any Bay 1 slab work; five-business-day notice to Lender of any SCDHEC communication; 30-day delivery of evidence of compliance on request; and no modification, termination, release or amendment of the LUR without Lender's consent. (ii) Confirm the Bank wants the LUR covenants in *both* the Mortgage and the Environmental Indemnity; the draft assumes belt-and-braces, as the commitment's closer note contemplates.

*Source:* Term Sheet §11.1(b), §11.2(b) (non-monetary defaults other than SPE, transfer and insurance defaults receive a 30-day cure, extendable to 90).

Suggested compromise if the Bank prefers: provide a 10-business-day cure for administrative breaches of Section 7.1(a) and (f), with no cure for slab penetration, residential use, LUR modification or a regulatory reopening. ### C. Leases, Rents and the Assignment

**C.1 — The assignment of rents has been converted to an absolute assignment, as instructed.**
*Source:* Kit's notes, ¶3; Term Sheet §5.2 (assignment "may be included within the Mortgage and Security Agreement or executed as a separate instrument, at the discretion of Lender's counsel"); Title Commitment Requirement 5 (expressly permits inclusion within the Mortgage).
*Observation.* The template's collateral assignment is insufficient under the assignment-of-rents statute Kit identifies, which gives an absolute assignment effect on execution (with enforcement triggered by default).
*Treatment.* Article IV of the Mortgage is drafted as an absolute and present assignment: "unconditionally, absolutely and presently grants, bargains, sells, conveys, transfers, assigns and sets over," with an express statement that it is "not merely a collateral assignment or an assignment as additional security." :::{.tight}

*Treatment.* Section 7.1 of the Mortgage implements the commitment's instruction directly and in detail: annual (and on-request) inspection of the Vapor Barrier by a qualified environmental professional acceptable to Lender, at Borrower's expense; no penetration or slab work without SCDHEC approval, notice to Lender and an approved repair plan; prohibition on residential use of Bay 1 (reinforced in Section 9.4(b)); advance written notice to SCDHEC of any Bay 1 slab work; five-business-day notice to Lender of any SCDHEC communication; 30-day delivery of evidence of compliance on request; and no modification, termination, release or amendment of the LUR without Lender's consent. Section 14.1(l) makes any breach an Event of Default.
*Action.* (i) Confirm the Environmental Indemnity (not in the record) contains the same provisions; Requirement 6 of the commitment will not be satisfied otherwise, and Lender should not accept an indemnity that addresses environmental liability generally but omits the vapor barrier and LUR obligations. (ii) Confirm the Bank wants the LUR covenants in *both* the Mortgage and the Environmental Indemnity; the draft assumes belt-and-braces, as the commitment's closer note contemplates.

**B.2 — Environmental defaults carry no cure period in the draft, which is defensible but should be a conscious decision.**
*Source:* Term Sheet §11.1(b), §11.2(b) (non-monetary defaults other than SPE, transfer and insurance defaults receive a 30-day cure, extendable to 90).
*Observation.* The Term Sheet does not list environmental defaults among the excepted categories, which would imply they get the standard 30-day cure. The title commitment's closer note, however, requires an event of default for LUR non-compliance, implying immediate consequence. The draft takes the middle course of making an environmental default an Event of Default (Section 14.1(l)) while Section 14.3(f) gives no cure period, consistent with the seriousness of the exposure and with the inability to "cure" a regulatory reopening.
*Action.* Confirm. A court may be receptive to a Borrower argument that a 30-day cure should apply to a curable environmental covenant (for example, a late inspection report). Suggested compromise if the Bank prefers: provide a 10-business-day cure for administrative breaches of Section 7.1(a) and (f), with no cure for slab penetration, residential use, LUR modification or a regulatory reopening. We have not included that compromise in the draft because it was not instructed.

**B.3 — The renovation will be performed directly over the Vapor Barrier, and the draw conditions do not currently require protection of it.**
*Source:* Phase I ESA §5.3(b), §5.4 and §6(c); Renovation Budget Line 1 (HVAC replacement) and Line 3 (façade restoration); Title Commitment closer note 1.
*Observation.* The Phase I ESA warns that any work affecting the Bay 1 floor slab must include inspection and repair of the vapor barrier with prior notice to SCDHEC, and recommends that the contractor be informed of its location. The Term Sheet's draw conditions (Section 8.4) do not mention the vapor barrier at all.
*Treatment.* Section 12.4(h) of the Mortgage adds a draw condition requiring contractor and subcontractor written acknowledgment of the Vapor Barrier and the LUR, and advance notice to SCDHEC of any Bay 1 slab work. Section 12.4(g)(iii) requires Lender consent for any change order involving Bay 1 slab work.
*Action.* This is an addition beyond the Term Sheet and is listed in Part IV for approval. There is no credit cost to it.

**B.4 — The Phase II waiver is documented only by reference and should be in the file.**
*Source:* Phase I ESA §6 (waiver "documented in correspondence dated January 22, 2025" between Marcus Prideaux and Clearfield).
*Observation.* The waiver letter itself is not in the record. Section 12.1(c) of the Term Sheet makes receipt of a satisfactory Phase I ESA (indicating "no recognized environmental conditions requiring remediation or further investigation, unless otherwise acceptable to Lender") a condition precedent. A CREC is not a REC, so the condition is satisfied on the report's face; the waiver is belt-and-braces.
*Treatment.* Section 7.1 of the Mortgage recites that Lender waived the Phase II requirement on the basis of the CREC status, the NFA determination and the recorded LUR. This converts an oral/administrative position into a documented acknowledgment by Borrower of the basis on which the Bank relied — which matters if environmental liability is later asserted.
*Action.* Obtain a copy of the January 22, 2025 correspondence for the file and confirm Marcus's description of it.

**B.5 — The SCDHEC remediation file has not been obtained.**
*Source:* Phase I ESA §6(a) (recommends the purchaser obtain and review the complete SCDHEC file including all sampling data, remediation reports, monitoring results and the NFA letter with all conditions).
*Observation.* Nothing in the record shows that the file has been obtained or reviewed by anyone other than the environmental consultant's summary.
*Treatment.* Section 3.4(d) of the Mortgage requires Borrower to deliver a complete copy of the SCDHEC file within ten business days after closing (or at closing if available).
*Action.* Recommend the Bank require delivery *before* closing, not after. If the NFA letter contains conditions beyond those summarized in the Phase I ESA, the Section 7.1 covenants may be incomplete. This is a due-diligence item, not a drafting item, and should be assigned to Marcus.

### C. Leases, Rents and the Assignment

**C.1 — The assignment of rents has been converted to an absolute assignment, as instructed.**
*Source:* Kit's notes, ¶3; Term Sheet §5.2 (assignment "may be included within the Mortgage and Security Agreement or executed as a separate instrument, at the discretion of Lender's counsel"); Title Commitment Requirement 5 (expressly permits inclusion within the Mortgage).
*Observation.* The template's collateral assignment is insufficient under the assignment-of-rents statute Kit identifies, which gives an absolute assignment effect on execution (with enforcement triggered by default).
*Treatment.* Article IV of the Mortgage is drafted as an absolute and present assignment: "unconditionally, absolutely and presently grants, bargains, sells, conveys, transfers, assigns and sets over," with an express statement that it is "not merely a collateral assignment or an assignment as additional security." Section 4.2 ties perfection to recording and enforcement to default. Section 4.3 grants Borrower a revocable license to collect until default, which is the market-standard way to preserve the absolute characterization while allowing the Borrower to operate. Section 4.4 permits direct notice to tenants on default without a court order or receiver. No separate Assignment of Leases and Rents will be recorded, satisfying both Term Sheet §5.2 and Title Requirement 5 by inclusion.
*Action.* Confirm the Bank is content with a single recorded instrument (it reduces recording cost and documentary stamp exposure, and it avoids a split-enforcement argument). Note that the Term Sheet's loan documents list at §14.3(c) contemplates a separate assignment; the draft supersedes that by election under §5.2.

**C.2 — Verify the statutory citation before the draft goes out.**
*Source:* Kit's notes, ¶3, citing "the Uniform Assignment of Rents Act (S.C. Code § 29-3-100 *et seq.*)."
*Observation.* The South Carolina enactment of the Uniform Assignment of Rents Act is cited in practice to Title 29, Chapter 3 of the South Carolina Code, and the section numbers should be verified against the current Code before they are printed in a recorded instrument. We have not independently confirmed the citation given in the markup notes.
*Treatment.* Article IV refers to "the Uniform Assignment of Rents Act as enacted in the State of South Carolina (the 'UARAA')" without a section citation. This is deliberate: a recorded instrument should not carry an unverified citation, and the operative effect does not depend on the citation.
*Action.* Have a paralegal pull the current Code sections and, if Kit confirms the citation, insert it at Section 4.2 in the next turn of the draft. This is a five-minute item and should not be allowed to hold up circulation.

**C.3 — The Lowcountry Lease has no assignment or subletting provision at all. This is the most important lease issue in the deal.**
*Source:* Rent Roll, Lease Abstracts (Bay 1: "No provision. Lease is silent on assignment or subletting rights and does not contain a consent requirement, prohibition, or landlord approval mechanism"); Appraisal §3.2 (appraiser notes the omission and does not opine on it); Kit's notes, ¶3 (three-step protocol).
*Observation.* As Kit notes, the statutory assignment is enforceable against the tenant on notification regardless of the lease's silence. The risk is practical: a tenant that never agreed to an assignment may resist or litigate at the moment of enforcement, and the tenant also has no contractual obligation to deliver an estoppel.
*Treatment.* All three steps in Kit's protocol are implemented:
:::{.tight}
(i) *Representation.* Section 4.5(b) of the Mortgage: Borrower warrants it has "good right, full power and lawful authority to absolutely assign the Leases and the Rents, including without limitation the Lowcountry Lease, notwithstanding the absence of any assignment, subletting or consent-to-assignment provision in the Lowcountry Lease."
(ii) *Estoppel as a condition precedent.* Section 4.7(a) records the Term Sheet condition (Section 12.1(j)) and states expressly that "Lender does not intend to waive such condition with respect to the Lowcountry Lease"; Section 4.7(c) adds a 90-day post-closing covenant to deliver a Lowcountry estoppel that acknowledges the Mortgage and the assignment, and agrees to pay Rents to Lender on notice after default.
(iii) *Lease amendment at the next opportunity.* Section 4.7(c) adds a commercially reasonable efforts covenant to obtain a customary assignment-consent provision at the next renewal, extension or amendment, and upon Lender's request after a default.
:::
*Action.* Marcus should know that the Lowcountry estoppel cannot be waived: the tenant has no contractual duty to give one, so if it is not obtained at closing, it may never be obtained. Recommend the Bank treat the Lowcountry estoppel as a hard closing condition and obtain it early — before closing, not in the last week. Also confirm whether the Lowcountry tenant has responded to any estoppel request already.

**C.4 — The Bay 2 right of first refusal is not a title exception and does not appear in the Term Sheet at all.**
*Source:* Rent Roll, Lease Abstracts (Harmon & Wren: ROFR on Bay 2; 15 business days to accept or decline; survives renewal); Rent Roll, Vacancy Schedule (Bay 2 marketing constrained; 30–60 day delay); Appraisal §3.2 and §6.3 (adds 60–90 days to absorption); Title Commitment Exception 6 (tenants "without any option to purchase or right of first refusal to purchase").
*Observation.* The ROFR is a *lease* right over Bay 2, not a purchase right, so the title exception is technically accurate. But it constrains the Bank's principal lease-up lever: a third-party offer for Bay 2 must first be presented to Harmon & Wren. The Term Sheet's DSCR covenant and its leasing covenant (Section 10.6) do not acknowledge it.
*Treatment.* Section 4.9 of the Mortgage requires compliance with the ROFR, delivery of any bona fide offer and any ROFR notice, and states that Lender takes no position on its enforceability or scope. Section 11.6 requires a quarterly leasing status report that addresses the ROFR while occupancy is below 90%. Exhibit B, item 5 discloses the ROFR as a Permitted Exception. Exhibit D, note 2 discloses it in the rent roll.
*Action.* No credit decision is required, but the Bank's lease-up timeline should be adjusted by 60–90 days, as the appraiser recommends. If the Bank intends to enforce any lease-up benchmark, that benchmark must be set with the ROFR in mind.

**C.5 — The Term Sheet requires estoppels and SNDAs from all tenants, and the leases make that harder for one tenant and easier for two.**
*Source:* Term Sheet §12.1(j), (k); Rent Roll, Lease Abstracts (Lowcountry: "Lease does not contain a provision requiring tenant to deliver estoppel certificates"; no SNDA provisions; Harmon & Wren: estoppel within 15 business days, subordinate with commercially reasonable non-disturbance; Tidemark: estoppel within 10 business days, agrees to execute SNDA on request).
*Observation.* Two of three tenants have contractual estoppel and subordination obligations. Lowcountry has neither. The Term Sheet treats all three identically.
*Treatment.* Sections 4.7(a)–(c) of the Mortgage carry the conditions precedent and add ongoing estoppel obligations; Section 4.7(b) requires an SNDA concurrently with any future lease.
*Action.* Confirm whether the Bank's standard SNDA form is acceptable to the tenants' lenders or franchisees (Lowcountry is a grocery; confirm whether it has a franchise or lender consent requirement). Start the SNDA circulation now.

**C.6 — Bay 3 expires on the same day the renovation must be complete, and its renewal notice deadline falls during construction.**
*Source:* Rent Roll, Lease Abstracts (Harmon & Wren expiration June 30, 2026; one three-year renewal at 95% of FMV with six months' notice, deadline December 31, 2025); Term Sheet §8.3 (Substantial Completion Deadline June 15, 2026); Rent Roll, Vacancy Schedule ("Bay 3 (At-Risk)").
*Observation.* The tenant's renewal decision is due December 31, 2025, in the middle of the renovation, with an expiration two weeks after substantial completion. If the tenant does not renew, the Property loses 3,800 square feet of ground-floor income at the very moment the DSCR test period begins, and the analysis in the rent roll shows the alternative (re-tenanting) costs $76,000 of TI and $28,500 of commissions.
*Treatment.* The Mortgage does not impose a lease-up or renewal covenant beyond Term Sheet §10.6 and the general leasing consent provisions in Section 4.8. Section 11.6 requires reporting.
*Action.* This is a credit monitoring item for the Bank. Recommend a covenant (not currently in the Term Sheet) requiring Borrower to deliver evidence of the renewal notice, or a copy of the renewal, within ten days after December 31, 2025. It is listed in Part IV as an optional addition.

**C.7 — The Tidemark lease gives the tenant disproportionate leverage over future leasing consents.**
*Source:* Rent Roll, Lease Abstracts (Tidemark: assignment requires consent "which may be withheld in Landlord's sole discretion"; two three-year renewals at FMV).
*Observation.* Not a defect, but note that Lender's consent standard under Section 4.8 of the Mortgage ("not unreasonably withheld, conditioned or delayed") is narrower than the landlord's own standard in the Tidemark lease. There is no conflict, because Lender's consent is a separate requirement from the landlord's.
*Treatment.* Section 4.8 as drafted; no change required.

{"command": "cd /workspace && cat > build/memo/03.md <<'EOF'
### D. Economics, Arithmetic and the Credit Structure

This group contains the findings that should be resolved before the draft is sent to the Bank, because three of them go to the structure of the Loan rather than to its documentation.

**D.1 — The 1.25x DSCR covenant is not achievable at any credible operating level of this Property.**
*Source:* Term Sheet §7.1 (minimum DSCR 1.25x; quarterly testing beginning after month 24; definitions of "Net Operating Income" and "Annual Debt Service" to be set in the Loan Documents); Term Sheet §3.6 (Daily SOFR + 2.85%, with a 3.00% SOFR floor, so a floor rate of 5.85%); Term Sheet §3.9 (25-year amortization from month 25); Rent Roll, Vacancy Schedule (pro forma NOI $622,772; debt service $1,122,000; DSCR 0.555x; conclusion that the covenant fails even in the best case); Rent Roll, Summary ("Current in-place NOI of ~$320,100 is insufficient to meet 1.25x DSCR").
*Observation.* Recomputation from source components (Part V, checks 12–16):
>*Annual interest at the floor rate:* $14,750,000 × 5.85% = **$862,875**.
>*Annual amortizing debt service* (25 years, 5.85%, beginning month 25): monthly payment **$93,674**, annual **$1,124,082**.
>*NOI required for 1.25x during the interest-only period:* **$1,078,594**.
>*NOI required for 1.25x after amortization begins:* **$1,405,103**.
>*Best-case stabilized NOI on the Borrower's own pro forma (all space leased by the test date):* **$622,772** → 0.72x interest-only, 0.55x amortizing.
>*In-place NOI:* approximately **$320,100** → 0.37x interest-only, 0.28x amortizing.
>*Debt yield at stabilization:* 4.2% ($622,772 ÷ $14,750,000).

The Loan is sized at $14,750,000 against NOI that, even at full stabilization and full escalation, supports roughly $9.5 million of debt at a 1.25x amortizing coverage test and roughly $8.6 million at 1.25x interest-only coverage. The DSCR covenant is therefore not a performance test; it is a scheduled default at the first test date.
*Treatment.* Sections 11.1 and 14.1(i) of the Mortgage implement the Term Sheet faithfully: 1.25x, tested quarterly on a trailing-twelve-month basis, with an Event of Default only after two consecutive failures. The Mortgage defines Net Operating Income and Debt Service as the Term Sheet delegates (Section 1.1), including a 4% management fee cap, a $0.25/SF replacement reserve deduction, and Lender's right to normalize non-recurring items, below-market rents and partial-year leases. No cure right is included, because none was instructed and inventing one would be a Borrower-favorable change the Bank has not approved. Section 11.1(d) adds a distribution lock-up below 1.10x, which is a partial, drafting-level mitigation on which the Bank should opine (Part IV).
*Action required — decision of the Bank.* The Bank must choose one of the following, and the draft will be conformed to the choice:
>::: {custom-style="Address"}
>(i) reduce the covenant to a level the Property can meet (but note that a covenant at or about 0.60x has no credit function); or
>(ii) extend the interest-only period beyond month 24 and accept a lower interim covenant, with the 1.25x test deferred to a stabilization date tied to occupancy (for example, the first quarter after the Property achieves 90% occupancy for two consecutive quarters); or
>(iii) retain 1.25x but add a contractual cure: Borrower may cure a failure by prepaying principal (without premium) or by depositing cash collateral with Lender in an amount sufficient to restore 1.25x for the applicable period; or
>(iv) retain 1.25x with no cure, and accept that the Loan will default at the first test date, which is only workable if the Bank intends to use the covenant as a renegotiation trigger.
>
>We recommend (iii). It preserves the covenant's credit function, gives the Bank a defined remedy other than foreclosure in a rising-rate or slow-lease-up scenario, and is straightforward to draft: a new Section 11.1(e) and a cross-reference in Section 14.3(d). If the Bank selects (i), (ii) or (iii), the Term Sheet should be amended before closing, because Section 7.1 states the 1.25x requirement as a bargained term and a Loan Document that departs from it invites a claim under Term Sheet §14.4 ("Lender reserves the right to require additional provisions ... provided that such additional provisions are not materially inconsistent with the terms of this Term Sheet").
:::

**D.2 — The appraisal's income approach does not support the concluded values, which undermines the as-stabilized loan-to-value ratio.**
*Source:* Appraiser's Report §6.2 (as-is NOI $332,000–$345,000; 6.25% cap rate), §6.3 (stabilized NOI $582,000–$592,000; 5.85% cap rate), §7 (concluded values $18,200,000 and $23,500,000), Key Ratios table (as-is LTV 81.04%; as-stabilized LTV 62.77%); Term Sheet §3.5 and §2.4.
*Observation.* Applying the appraiser's own capitalization rates to the appraiser's own net operating income produces values that do not approximate the conclusions:

| Scenario | NOI relied on | Capitalization rate | Value indicated | Value concluded | Implied cap rate on concluded value |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| As-is | $332,000–$345,000 | 6.25% | $5,312,000–$5,520,000 | $18,200,000 | 1.82%–1.90% |
| As-stabilized | $582,000–$592,000 | 5.85% | $9,949,000–$10,120,000 | $23,500,000 | 2.48%–2.52% |

The sales comparison approach is internally coherent ($600, $550 and $620 per square foot for three 2024–2025 comparables, against $587 per square foot as-is). The income approach is not. The appraiser states that it reconciled the income approach with the sales comparison and cost approaches, but the summary report does not disclose how, and the addenda that might explain it are not in the record.
*Treatment.* The Mortgage does not restate appraised values, and correctly does not — an instrument should not incorporate a valuation that may change. The consequences are recorded here rather than in the document.
*Action required — decision of the Bank.* (i) Obtain the complete appraisal with all addenda, and specifically the discounted cash flow analysis the appraiser says supports the conclusion. (ii) Consider ordering a review appraisal under the Bank's own policy; the discrepancy is of a magnitude (a factor of roughly 2.3x between income-approach value and concluded value) that a reviewer will raise. (iii) Until this is resolved, the Bank should not rely on the 62.77% as-stabilized loan-to-value ratio for credit approval or for any covenant keyed to value. (iv) Note also that the as-is ratio of 81.04% exceeds a customary 65%–75% range; Kit's closing note asks Marcus to confirm whether the loan committee has approved exceptions for this Loan, and this memorandum repeats that request in writing (Part VIII).

**D.3 — Occupancy is stated as 68% in two documents and is 56.13% on the verified rent roll; in-place rent is stated at $415,100 and is approximately $422,966 after scheduled escalations.**
*Source:* Term Sheet §2.3 ("Current occupancy is approximately sixty-eight percent (68%)" and, in the same paragraph, "Vacant space consists of Bay 2 ... and 2nd Floor Suite B ..., totaling 13,600 square feet, or approximately 43.9% of total building area"); Appraisal §1 and §3.1 ("68% (21,400 SF of 31,000 SF occupied)"; "vacant area is 13,600 SF (32%)"); Rent Roll, Summary (17,400 SF occupied; 56.13%; 13,600 SF vacant; 43.87%); Rent Roll, Lease Abstracts (rent escalation schedules).
*Observation.* The Term Sheet contradicts itself in a single paragraph: 68% occupancy and 43.9% vacancy cannot both be true. The rent roll is correct: occupied area is Bay 1 (3,800) + Bay 3 (3,800) + Suite A (9,800) = 17,400 SF = 56.13%; vacant is 13,600 SF = 43.87%. The appraisal's supporting sentence ("21,400 SF of 31,000 SF occupied ... 13,600 SF (32%)") does not add to 31,000 at all (21,400 + 13,600 = 35,000), and 21,400 ÷ 31,000 is 69.03%, not 68%. Separately, the rent roll's "Base Rent (Current)" column has not been updated for the escalations its own escalation schedules describe:

| Space | Stated current rent | Escalation per lease abstract | Rent in effect on April 15, 2025 | Annualized |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bay 1 | $28.50/SF ($108,300) | 3% each January 1 from January 1, 2025 → $29.36/SF | $29.36/SF (or $28.50 × 1.03 = $29.36) | $111,549 |
| Bay 3 | $24.00/SF ($91,200) | 2.5% each July 1 from July 1, 2023 → $24.60 (2023), $25.22 (2024) | $25.22/SF | $95,837 |
| Suite A | $22.00/SF ($215,600) | 2.5% each April 1 from April 1, 2026 | $22.00/SF | $215,600 |
| Total | $415,100 | | | **$422,986** |

The rent roll's own "Realistic Scenario" line uses $422,700 for the same three occupied spaces, confirming that the Summary tab figure is stale rather than a different assumption.
*Treatment.* Exhibit D of the Mortgage presents the rent roll as delivered, with a note requiring Borrower to deliver at closing a certified rent roll conformed for all scheduled escalations, and making that certification a representation under Section 6.3. Section 4.5(a) warrants that the rent roll is true and correct as of the Closing Date. We have not restated the term sheet's 68% figure anywhere in the Mortgage, and the draft does not repeat it. Exhibit D also states the correct occupancy of 56.13%.
*Action.* (i) Ask Borrower's counsel to confirm the rent actually invoiced for January 2025 (Bay 1) and July 2024 (Bay 3) — the escalation clauses may be drafted so that the rent adjusting mechanism operates differently from the schedule in the abstract, and only the ledgers settle it. (ii) Correct the occupancy figure in the credit approval memorandum and in any investor or rating presentation; a 12-point overstatement of occupancy in a loan file is the kind of error that is remembered after a default. (iii) Note that correcting the rent upward does not materially change the DSCR conclusion in D.1 (it improves stabilized NOI by roughly $8,000).

**D.4 — Sources and uses do not balance once closing costs and the required reserve deposit are included.**
*Source:* Term Sheet §3.4 (Total Project Cost $20,950,000; Borrower equity $6,200,000, "representing approximately 29.6% of the Total Project Cost"); Term Sheet §3.3(a) (Initial Advance "to be applied toward the purchase price, closing costs, and funded reserves"); Term Sheet §6.3 ($150,000 tenant improvement and leasing commission reserve deposited by Borrower at closing); Term Sheet §13.1 (origination fee $147,500); Term Sheet §13.2 (Borrower pays all closing costs); Kit's notes, ¶6 (documentary stamp tax 0.37% = $54,575).
*Observation.* The stated Total Project Cost is exactly the sum of the Loan and the equity contribution ($17,800,000 + $3,150,000 = $20,950,000 = $14,750,000 + $6,200,000). It therefore contains no allowance for:

| Item | Amount | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Loan origination fee (1.00%) | $147,500 | Term Sheet §13.1 |
| South Carolina documentary stamp tax on the Mortgage (0.37%) | $54,575 | Kit's notes ¶6; S.C. recording schedule |
| Tenant improvement and leasing commission reserve | $150,000 | Term Sheet §6.3 |
| Title insurance premium and endorsements | not quantified in record | Term Sheet §13.2(d), §5.6 |
| ALTA/NSPS survey | not quantified | Term Sheet §13.2(e) |
| Appraisal, Phase I ESA, and any review | not quantified | Term Sheet §13.2(b), (c) |
| Lender's legal fees (Fielding, Ashworth & Cole LLP) | not quantified | Term Sheet §13.2(a) |
| **Quantified subtotal** | **$352,075** | |

The equity contribution of $6,200,000 is itself committed by the Members in fixed proportions ($4,464,000 / $1,116,000 / $620,000) under Operating Agreement §2.2, so an additional call requires either a further capital call or a reallocation of the Initial Advance — which would reduce the cash available to the seller at closing and leave the purchase price unfunded.
*Treatment.* The Mortgage does not restate project cost (correct for an instrument). Section 17.11 places all recording, documentary stamp, title and closing costs on Borrower, consistent with the Term Sheet, and Section 12.1(m)-type evidence of equity funding is carried as a closing condition under the Term Sheet rather than a Mortgage covenant.
*Action required.* Confirm with Marcus how closing costs and the $150,000 reserve deposit are funded. Three possibilities: (i) the equity contribution is in fact larger than $6,200,000 and the Operating Agreement summary is out of date; (ii) the Bank is funding the origination fee and reserve out of Loan proceeds, which reduces the cash to the seller and requires the seller's consent; or (iii) the shortfall is being met from Borrower's operating cash outside the committed capital. The draft assumes (iii) and does not condition disbursement on a sources-and-uses statement, but the Bank's closing checklist should, and we recommend adding one.

**D.5 — Tenant improvement and leasing commission costs are budgeted three times over.**
*Source:* Renovation Budget Line 4 ($550,000 "Tenant Improvement Allowances" for Bay 2 and Suite B, "budgeted at ~$40.44/SF blended"); Rent Roll, Vacancy Schedule (TI allowance assumed $25.00/SF for Bay 2 = $95,000 and $22.00/SF for Suite B = $215,600; aggregate $310,600; leasing commissions $89,750); Term Sheet §6.3 ($150,000 separate TI/LC reserve funded at closing).
*Observation.* Three different buckets address the same cost: $550,000 inside the Renovation Budget, $310,600 in the lease-up schedule, and $150,000 in a separate reserve, with no stated interaction. The renovation budget line ($40.44/SF blended) is 78% higher than the lease-up schedule's assumption ($22.81/SF blended: $310,600 ÷ 13,600 SF). Separately, Line 4 is described as "Various (to be contracted per lease terms)" in the budget detail and yet is included in the GC Contract sum of $2,850,000, as discussed in D.10.
*Treatment.* Exhibit C of the Mortgage reproduces the Renovation Budget as delivered, allocates the Line 4 amount between the Renovation Holdback ($450,000) and Borrower equity ($100,000), and adds a note requiring the scope of the GC Contract — including whether Line 4 sits inside or outside it — to be confirmed by the executed contract and change orders. Section 12.3 preserves the separate $150,000 reserve and its 30-day replenishment obligation, which is the only one of the three that gives the Bank a replenishment right.
*Action.* Ask Borrower to reconcile the three figures and to state which costs are funded from the Renovation Holdback, which from the reserve, and which from Borrower equity. If Line 4 is in truth $310,600 rather than $550,000, then either the Renovation Budget is overstated by $239,400 (which weakens the 71.43% holdback ratio and the as-stabilized value assumption) or the excess is available for other costs. This must be resolved before the Bank approves the draw schedule, because the draw conditions in Section 12.4 are tied to the Line 4 allocation.

**D.6 — The DSCR test date is stated three different ways.**

The Mortgage defines Net Operating Income and Debt Service as the Term Sheet delegates (Section 1.1), including a 4% management fee cap, a $0.25/SF replacement reserve deduction, and Lender's right to normalize non-recurring items, below-market rents and partial-year leases. No cure right is included, because none was instructed and inventing one would be a Borrower-favorable change the Bank has not approved. Section 11.1(d) adds a distribution lock-up below 1.10x, which is a partial, drafting-level mitigation on which the Bank should opine (Part IV).
*Action required — decision of the Bank.* The Bank must choose one of the following, and the draft will be conformed to the choice:
>::: {custom-style="Address"}
>(i) reduce the covenant to a level the Property can meet (but note that a covenant at or about 0.60x has no credit function); or
>(ii) extend the interest-only period beyond month 24 and accept a lower interim covenant, with the 1.25x test deferred to a stabilization date tied to occupancy (for example, the first quarter after the Property achieves 90% occupancy for two consecutive quarters); or
>(iii) retain 1.25x but add a contractual cure: Borrower may cure a failure by prepaying principal (without premium) or by depositing cash collateral with Lender in an amount sufficient to restore 1.25x for the applicable period; or
>(iv) retain 1.25x with no cure, and accept that the Loan will default at the first test date, which is only workable if the Bank intends to use the covenant as a renegotiation trigger.
>
>We recommend (iii). It preserves the covenant's credit function, gives the Bank a defined remedy other than foreclosure in a rising-rate or slow-lease-up scenario, and is straightforward to draft: a new Section 11.1(e) and a cross-reference in Section 14.3(d). If the Bank selects (i), (ii) or (iii), the Term Sheet should be amended before closing, because Section 7.1 states the 1.25x requirement as a bargained term and a Loan Document that departs from it invites a claim under Term Sheet §14.4 ("Lender reserves the right to require additional provisions ... provided that such additional provisions are not materially inconsistent with the terms of this Term Sheet").
:::

**D.2 — The appraisal's income approach does not support the concluded values, which undermines the as-stabilized loan-to-value ratio.**
